planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall into well-drained, average, prairie-type soil in full sun to partial shade; Nuttall's pleatleaf is native to Texas Hill Country and adjacent prairie and blooms later in spring than the similar Nemastylis geminiflora, going fully dormant through summer heat.

directions: Plant corms 2 to 3 inches deep in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Nuttall's pleatleaf is a Texas Hill Country and prairie native closely related to the more widespread prairie celestial but taller in stature, with a few pleated, grass-like leaves and sky-blue, three-petaled flowers that open for a single morning at a time over a spring bloom season lasting several weeks. Like its relative it goes fully summer-dormant after flowering and setting seed, disappearing underground until the following late winter, so plant it where the gap can be filled by later-emerging prairie grasses or perennials. It performs best in a naturalistic prairie or rock-garden setting with average, well-drained soil rather than a rich, heavily amended border, echoing the lean limestone soils of its native range.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination, or plant container-grown divisions in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun in spring; white blue-eyed grass is a prairie and glade species that tolerates drier, leaner soil than the more common blue-flowered Sisyrinchium species.

directions: Direct sow in fall or plant container divisions in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; white blue-eyed grass grows in tallgrass prairies, limestone glades, and open woodland edges across the central and eastern US, producing the same grass-like, iris-family foliage as its blue-flowered relatives but with delicate white to pale lavender, yellow-centered flowers opening in mid-spring. It tolerates drier, leaner soil than the more common blue-eyed grass species, making it a good fit for a sunny prairie planting or rock garden rather than a consistently moist border. It self-seeds modestly in favorable open, sunny conditions, gradually forming small drifts, and combines well with other spring prairie natives like prairie phlox and golden alexanders.

subcategory: Gulf Coast native spring iris-family corm

planting.note: Plant small corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; propeller flower is native to the coastal prairies and open grasslands of Texas and Louisiana, blooming through late spring and summer with flowers that each open for only a single afternoon.

directions: Plant corms in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; propeller flower is a striking Gulf Coast native iris relative of Texas and Louisiana prairies, producing wiry stems topped with unusual, pinwheel-shaped flowers whose three narrow, twisted outer petals are deep maroon-purple mottled with cream and yellow at the base, giving the bloom a distinctive spinning-propeller look unlike any other native wildflower. Each flower opens for a single afternoon, but a healthy corm produces a long succession of blooms from late spring into summer, longer than most of its spring-only iris-family relatives. Adapted to the region's hot, humid summers and mild winters, it is an excellent, low-maintenance choice for a Gulf Coast prairie or native wildflower planting in lean, well-drained soil, needing little supplemental water once established.
